sections.b: Jubilees 49 gathers the Passover rules of Exodus 12, Numbers 9 and Deuteronomy 16 into one law dictated to Moses and "engraved on the heavenly tablets" (Jubilees 49:8). The lamb is slaughtered on the fourteenth of the first month at the edge of evening, eaten that night until "the third part of the night" (Jubilees 49:10-12), roasted, never boiled, with no bone broken, "For no bone of the Israelites will be crushed" (Jubilees 49:13). Once there is a sanctuary, it may be eaten only in its courtyard, by men twenty and older (Jubilees 49:16-21). The date may never move (Jubilees 49:7; 49:14). In Egypt it was "all the powers of Mastema" that struck the firstborn and passed over the houses with blood (Jubilees 49:2-4), and Israel ate and drank wine, one of the earliest mentions of wine at the meal (Charles 1902).

common: The Passover was kept in homes in Egypt but at the one sanctuary in the land (Deuteronomy 16:5-7); Jubilees takes the second rule and makes it stricter.
uncommon: Jubilees ties the Passover to a fixed date in a 364-day calendar, so that it falls on the same day of the week every year.

sections.h: Jubilees' last chapter: the Sabbath law
sections.b: Jubilees ends with the Sabbath, as its creation story began with it (Jubilees 2:17-33). Chapter 50 makes death the penalty for any Sabbath work (Exodus 31:14-15; Exodus 35:2) and spells out what counts: travel, buying and selling, drawing water not prepared on the sixth day, carrying out of a tent or house, lying with one's wife, farming, lighting a fire, riding, sailing, hunting and killing, fasting and making war (Jubilees 50:8; 50:12). The only work allowed is the sanctuary's offerings (Jubilees 50:10-11; compare Matthew 12:5). The day is for eating, drinking and blessing God, "a day of the holy kingdom for all Israel" (Jubilees 50:9). Charles 1902 read the ban on war against the early Maccabean years (1 Maccabees 2:29-41).
sections.refs: Jubilees 50:6-13; Exodus 16:22-30; Exodus 31:12-17; Exodus 35:2-3; 1 Maccabees 2:29-41; Mark 2:27

common: Jubilees is one of the strictest ancient Jewish Sabbath codes, stricter than the Bible and in places stricter than the Mishnah.
uncommon: Its ban on marital relations on the Sabbath, rejected by the rabbis, was kept by the Samaritans, the Karaites and the Beta Israel (Charles 1902).

sections.h: Fifty jubilees from Adam to the Jordan
sections.b: Jubilees counts history in jubilees of forty-nine years and closes with the sum: "forty-nine jubilees from the days of Adam to this day, and one week of years and two years," with forty more years until Israel crosses the Jordan (Jubilees 50:4). That is the year 2410 at Sinai and 2450 at the Jordan, exactly fifty jubilees. The laws of the land's Sabbaths and jubilees were told on Sinai (Leviticus 25:1), but the year to begin counting was held back until Israel entered the land (Jubilees 50:2-3). The jubilees will go on "until Israel is made clean" (Jubilees 50:5). Charles 1902 notes that a 49-year jubilee was a minority view among Jewish writers, most of whom counted fifty (Leviticus 25:10).

Jubilees 47-48 tells Moses' story to Moses himself. It adds dates (born in the year 2330 from creation, at court at 21, fled at 42, back in Egypt at 80), names (his mother Jochebed, his sister Miriam, Pharaoh's daughter Tarmut), and details: his mother was reported, left him in the ark seven days and nursed him by night (Jubilees 47:3-4). His father Amram taught him writing (Jubilees 47:9), unlike Acts 7:22. On his way back to Egypt it was Prince Mastema, not the LORD (Exodus 4:24), who tried to kill him, and the angel of the presence rescued him (Jubilees 48:2-4).

In Jubilees, Prince Mastema stands behind the enemies of the Exodus. He tries to kill Moses on the road (Jubilees 48:2-3, where Exodus 4:24 has the LORD), helps Pharaoh's sorcerers (Jubilees 48:9), and is bound from the fourteenth to the eighteenth of the first month so that he cannot accuse Israel, then loosed so the Egyptians will pursue (Jubilees 48:15-18). Charles 1902 reads the "he" who hardens the Egyptians' hearts at the sea as Mastema (Jubilees 48:17), and "all the powers of Mastema" are sent to kill the firstborn (Jubilees 49:2). Yet he acts only as God allows. Compare the accuser of Revelation 12:10 and the binding in Revelation 20:2-3.
sections.refs: Jubilees 48:2-18; Jubilees 49:2; Exodus 4:24; Exodus 14:8; 1 Chronicles 21:1; Revelation 12:10; Revelation 20:2-3

common: Jubilees, like 1 Chronicles 21:1, moves a troubling act from God to an evil spirit.

sections.b: Jubilees uses the common noun säyṭan, "adversary" or "accuser," for a state of the world: while Joseph lived there was "no satan and nothing evil" (Jubilees 46:2), and when Israel is made clean "It will no longer have any satan or any evil one" (Jubilees 50:5). The leader of the evil spirits in the Exodus chapters is Mastema; see that topic.

Jubilees does not name Pharaoh's magicians, but it explains their power: Prince Mastema "helped the sorcerers of Egypt, and they stood against you" (Jubilees 48:9). The angels let them do harm but not heal (Jubilees 48:10), and after the sores struck them, they could do no more signs (Jubilees 48:11; Exodus 9:11). 2 Timothy 3:8 uses the same picture: "Jannes and Jambres stood against Moses."

Jubilees 48:5 lists all ten plagues in one sentence, in Exodus' order except that the sores come before the death of the animals. Jubilees calls them "Ten great and terrible judgments" (Jubilees 48:7), done for Israel's sake by the covenant with Abraham (Jubilees 48:8; Genesis 15:14), and it ends with the Lord burning Egypt's gods (Jubilees 48:5; compare Exodus 12:12). A thousand Egyptians died at the sea for every Hebrew baby drowned (Jubilees 48:14), a measure-for-measure punishment like that of Wisdom of Solomon 11:16 and 18:5.
sections.refs: Jubilees 48:5-14; Exodus 7:14-12:30; Genesis 15:14; Wisdom of Solomon 18:5

sections.b: Jubilees counts Joseph's 110 years as seventeen in Canaan, ten as a slave, three in prison and eighty ruling Egypt (Jubilees 46:3). While he lived there was "no satan and nothing evil" (Jubilees 46:2). It explains why his bones waited for Moses (Exodus 13:19): a war between Egypt and Canaan shut the border, so Egypt would not again carry a body to Canaan (Jubilees 46:6-7). His brothers' bones were later taken to the double cave at Hebron (Jubilees 46:9).

Jubilees says that during a war between Egypt and Canaan the Israelites carried the bones of all Jacob's sons except Joseph to "the double cave" near Hebron, and that some stayed in the hill country of Hebron, Moses' father Amram among them (Jubilees 46:9-10). Charles 1902 notes the same tradition in the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs and Josephus, and thought Stephen's words in Acts 7:15-16 depend on it, though Stephen names Shechem.

Jubilees names Moses' sister at the river, which Exodus 2 does not, and gives her a task: for seven days, while her mother nursed the baby at night, "by day your sister Miriam guarded you from the birds" (Jubilees 47:4). She then offers to fetch a Hebrew nurse, as in Exodus 2:7.

Exodus says the LORD struck Egypt's firstborn and kept "the destroyer" out of Israel's houses (Exodus 12:23; Exodus 12:29). Jubilees says "all the powers of Mastema were sent out to kill every firstborn," from Pharaoh's firstborn to that of the captive slave woman at the mill, and passed over every house with blood on its doorway (Jubilees 49:2-4).

In Jubilees the angel of the presence stands between Moses, the Egyptians and Israel, and the Lord brings Israel "through the middle of the sea as if through dry land" (Jubilees 48:13). Mastema, loosed on the nineteenth day, urges the Egyptians on, and they are thrown "into the depths of the abyss" (Jubilees 48:14-17). Jubilees dates the seven days of unleavened bread to the march, finished "on the shore of the sea" (Jubilees 49:23).

Exodus 14:8 says "The LORD made the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt stubborn." Jubilees, after Mastema's powers are loosed, says "He hardened their hearts," yet adds that the Egyptians "were made bold by the Lord our God, so that he could strike" them (Jubilees 48:16-17). Charles 1902 read the "he" as Mastema. The book keeps God in control while placing the hardening one step away.

sections.h: The Passover only at the sanctuary (Jubilees 49)
sections.b: Jubilees forbids the Passover "in their towns or in any place except before the Lord's tabernacle, or else before the house where his name has come to live" (Jubilees 49:21), first at the tabernacle set up in the land and then at the temple (Jubilees 49:18-20). It follows Deuteronomy 16:5-7 and goes further: the meat must be eaten in the sanctuary's courtyard (Jubilees 49:20), where the Mishnah later allowed all Jerusalem (Charles 1902).

Jubilees 50 takes the death penalty of Exodus 31:14-15 and Exodus 35:2 and applies it to every item in its long list of Sabbath offenses, from travel and trade to marital relations, fasting and war (Jubilees 50:8; 50:12-13).

Because the Sabbath is a feast "to eat, to drink and to be full" (Jubilees 50:10), Jubilees counts fasting on it a capital offense (Jubilees 50:12). Judith keeps the same rule: she fasted every day "except the days before the Sabbaths and the Sabbaths" (Judith 8:6).

Jubilees forbids making war on the Sabbath on pain of death (Jubilees 50:12). Early in the Maccabean revolt about a thousand Jews died rather than fight on the Sabbath (1 Maccabees 2:38), and Mattathias then allowed defense (1 Maccabees 2:41). Charles 1902 read Jubilees' rule as the strict view of those years.

Jubilees insists that the Passover be kept "once a year on its day" and never moved "from one day to another, or from one month to another" (Jubilees 49:7; 49:14), because it is "engraved on the heavenly tablets" (Jubilees 49:8). In the book's year of exactly 364 days, every date falls on the same weekday each year, so a fixed day is possible.
